title: ABC Manufacturing: cash control training, bank reconciliation, petty cash and service charge entries
participant_role: Controller (head accountant) for ABC Manufacturing training a newly hired accountant
judge_role: Newly hired accountant for ABC Manufacturing who will take over cash control duties
scenario:
You are to assume the role of controller (head accountant) for ABC manufacturing. You have just hired an accountant (judge) to handle some of your duties, including controlling the cash account. Your job is to train the new accountant (judge) on how to perform basic cash control procedures.

According to your records, the company has the following:

Balance of cash in Checkbook (stub 134): $14,300
Total Outstanding Checks: $2,000
Total Outstanding Deposits: $4,000
Service Charge: $50
Balance of cash on Bank Statement (12/31/13): $12,250

Demonstrate to the new accountant (judge) how to reconcile a bank account in order to prove cash. In addition to explaining all necessary cash control procedures and the benefits of EFT, you should demonstrate to the new accountant (judge) how to journalize establishment of petty cash fund of $200 and bank service charge entries.

You will conduct your training in the new accountant's (judge's) office. The new accountant (judge) will begin the role play by greeting you as you enter his/her office. You will proceed to provide training in cash control systems. After you have conducted your training and answered the new accountant's (judge's) questions, the new accountant (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your help.
tasks: Demonstrate to the new accountant (judge) how to reconcile a bank account in order to prove cash
Explain all necessary cash control procedures
Demonstrate how to journalize establishment of petty cash fund of $200
Demonstrate how to journalize bank service charge entries

solution.overview: A strong answer walks the new accountant through a two-column bank reconciliation that proves cash at $14,250 on both sides, explains why cash needs controls because it is the most liquid asset, lists specific procedures, journalizes the $200 petty cash fund and the $50 service charge, and closes with the time and cost benefits of EFT.

answer: Cash is the most liquid asset, so it is the easiest to lose or steal and needs formal procedures
Reconcile the bank account every month
Use restrictive endorsements on checks received ("For deposit only")
Keep signature cards on file and require check approval before signing
Deposit cash promptly and establish a petty cash fund for small purchases
Start with the checkbook balance of $14,300 and deduct the $50 service charge: adjusted checkbook balance $14,250
Start with the bank statement balance of $12,250, add outstanding deposits of $4,000 and subtract outstanding checks of $2,000: adjusted bank balance $14,250
Both adjusted balances equal $14,250, so cash is proved
Even a difference of a few cents must be investigated because it may be the tip of a larger problem
Debit Petty Cash $200 and credit Cash $200
Petty cash lets the business pay for small, immaterial items without writing a check
Debit Miscellaneous Expense $50 and credit Cash $50
This entry brings the checkbook balance down to the adjusted balance of $14,250
Saves time because no checks have to be written
Reduces the lag between paying and the payment clearing the bank
Cuts postage and check printing fees

judge_question_answers.question: Does it really matter if the bank reconciliation is only off a few cents?
answer: Yes, even a small difference could be the tip of the iceberg
A few cents may point to a much larger error or a control problem that must be found

judge_question_answers.question: What is the need for a petty cash account?
answer: Petty cash is used for small transactions
It lets the business avoid writing a check for immaterial purchases

judge_question_answers.question: How do you determine if a check is outstanding?
answer: A check is outstanding if it has been written but has not yet cleared the bank
Start with the checkbook and compare it to the bank statement to see which checks cleared and which did not

key_concepts.definition: A schedule that explains the difference between the checkbook balance and the bank statement balance. Adjusted checkbook balance (checkbook balance minus service charges and other bank deductions) must equal adjusted bank balance (bank balance plus outstanding deposits minus outstanding checks).
Showing that the cash recorded in the books agrees with the actual cash in the bank after reconciling items are considered.
A check the business has written and recorded but that has not yet cleared the bank, so it is subtracted from the bank statement balance.
A deposit the business has recorded that the bank has not yet added to the statement, so it is added to the bank statement balance.
A fee the bank deducts from the account. It is recorded with a debit to Miscellaneous Expense and a credit to Cash after the reconciliation reveals it.
A small amount of cash kept on hand to pay for minor expenses. Establishing it is recorded as a debit to Petty Cash and a credit to Cash.
Internal controls that protect cash because it is so liquid: monthly bank reconciliations, restrictive endorsements, signature cards, check approval, prompt deposits and a petty cash fund.
Writing "For deposit only" on the back of a received check so it can only be deposited into the company account and not cashed by someone else.
Moving money between bank accounts electronically instead of by paper check, which saves time, shortens clearing delays and reduces postage and check costs.
